option_description: Controls whether sensitivity or classification labels (e.g., CONFIDENTIAL, SECRET, RESTRICTED) are mandatorily applied to SIEM incident records at the platform level. Determines if labeling is automatic at ingestion, left to analyst discretion, or entirely absent.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'incident_data_misclassification' when this value is 'none' (unconditionally) or 'optional' combined with disabled export controls, or when role restriction is broad/unrestricted and labeling is not enforced. Without enforced labels, incident records containing IOCs, attacker TTPs, and victim data are treated as general operational data, enabling inadvertent sharing or storage without appropriate handling controls. Maps to MITRE T1530 (Data from Cloud Storage) where misclassified data in cloud repositories lacks protective controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk SIEM, navigate to Settings > Data Classification Policies or Enterprise Security > Incident Management Settings and check if a mandatory classification field is configured on the incident schema. In Microsoft Sentinel, go to Settings > Workspace Settings > Data Classification and inspect whether sensitivity labels from Microsoft Purview are enforced on incident entities.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Settings > Incident Management > Notable Event Settings | Sentinel: Settings > Workspace Settings > Microsoft Purview Integration
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A mandatory classification field present in the incident record schema with no option to save without a label selected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Splunk REST API to inspect the notable events data model and check if a 'classification' or 'sensitivity_label' field is defined as required. For Microsoft Sentinel, use the Azure REST API to retrieve incident schema and check label enforcement policies.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS https://<splunk-host>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/configs/conf-es_notable_settings | grep -i 'classif\|sensitivity\|label'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response contains a required classification field definition; absence indicates labeling is optional or unconfigured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the SIEM host, inspect the incident management configuration files for label enforcement settings. For Splunk ES, review the notable event configuration. For IBM QRadar, inspect the offense management configuration XML.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'sensitivity\|classification\|label' /opt/splunk/etc/apps/SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite/default/es_notable_settings.conf
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 'required = true' or equivalent mandatory label setting present in the configuration; missing entry means labeling is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SIEM administrator and SOC lead to determine whether a classification policy exists in documentation, whether analysts are required to apply labels before closing incidents, and whether the platform technically prevents label-free incident submission.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation of a mandatory labeling procedure with evidence of technical enforcement (e.g., required field, automated ingestion tagging workflow, DLP integration).

option_description: Controls whether the SIEM platform enforces DLP policies, approval workflows, or sharing restrictions that prevent analysts from freely exporting, forwarding, or distributing incident reports to external parties or unsanctioned destinations.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'incident_data_misclassification' when labeling is 'optional' AND export controls are disabled. Without export controls, analysts can exfiltrate full incident records — including active IOCs, unpatched vulnerability details, and victim identities — to personal email, cloud storage, or external ticketing systems with no audit trail or approval gate. This directly enables T1530 (Data from Cloud Storage) risk by allowing sensitive investigation data to land in uncontrolled cloud repositories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, navigate to Settings > Alert Actions and Data Exports to review which export destinations are permitted without restriction. In Microsoft Sentinel, navigate to Settings > Analytics > Export Rules and check if export connectors require approval workflows. In IBM QRadar, check Admin > System Settings > Offense Export Controls.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Settings > Data Inputs > Export Policies | Sentinel: Content Hub > Export Settings | QRadar: Admin > Authorized Services > Export Controls
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export destinations restricted to approved endpoints, with approval workflow required for new destinations or ad-hoc exports.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM API to enumerate configured export rules and check for unrestricted export endpoints. For Sentinel, use the Azure Monitor REST API to list data export rules and confirm destination restrictions.
how_to_obtain.command: az monitor log-analytics workspace data-export list --resource-group <rg> --workspace-name <workspace> --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export rules listed show only approved internal destinations (e.g., secured storage account); unrestricted destinations flag this as false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SIEM sharing and forwarding policy documentation. Determine whether an approval ticket is required before an analyst can export incident data, and whether DLP tools intercept and block unauthorized exports at the network or endpoint level.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written export policy with documented approval chain, evidence of DLP rule blocking SIEM data exports to personal email or unmanaged cloud storage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM audit logs for export and forwarding events over the past 90 days. Identify whether exports occurred without approval records, and whether any exports went to external or uncontrolled destinations.
how_to_obtain.command: index=_audit action=export OR action=share OR action=forward sourcetype=splunk_audit | table _time, user, action, dest | head 100
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All export events correlated with a corresponding approval ticket; absence of unapproved export events to external destinations.

option_description: Defines the scope of role-based access control applied to SIEM incident records, determining whether read/write access is limited to dedicated security personnel (SOC analysts, IR teams), broadly available to operational IT staff (helpdesk, NOC, IT operations), or entirely unrestricted to all authenticated users.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'incident_data_misclassification' when this is 'broad_operational' or 'unrestricted' and labeling is not enforced. It also triggers 'pii_not_masked_in_incident_records' when the value is 'unrestricted'. Broad or unrestricted access exposes raw incident data — including victim identities, unpatched CVEs, and active attacker infrastructure — to roles without security training or need-to-know. Enables T1213 (Data from Information Repositories) where any authenticated user can query incident repositories. MITRE T1212 (Exploitation for Credential Access) risk increases as credentials embedded in incident tickets become accessible to broader staff.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, navigate to Settings > Access Controls > Roles and review which roles have access to the 'notable_events' index or ES dashboards. In Microsoft Sentinel, navigate to Access Control (IAM) on the Log Analytics Workspace and inspect role assignments for SecurityReader or Contributor roles assigned to non-security groups.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Access Controls > Roles > Review 'indexes_allowed' for notable_events | Sentinel: Log Analytics Workspace > Access Control (IAM) > Role Assignments
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only dedicated security roles (SOC_Analyst, IR_Engineer, SecurityEngineer) listed with access to incident data indexes/workspaces.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk, query the REST API to list all roles with access to the notable_events or siem_incidents index. For Microsoft Sentinel, use Azure CLI to enumerate role assignments on the workspace.
how_to_obtain.command: az role assignment list --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/<workspace> --output table | grep -v 'SecurityTeam\|SOC'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No non-security roles (e.g., ITOperations, Helpdesk, NOC) listed with SecurityReader or higher permissions on the SIEM workspace.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Splunk REST API for role capability and index access assignments to identify non-security roles with incident data access.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS 'https://<splunk>:8089/services/authorization/roles?output_mode=json' | python3 -c "import sys,json; roles=json.load(sys.stdin)['entry']; [print(r['name'], r['content'].get('srchIndexesAllowed','')) for r in roles]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only security-designated roles show 'notable_events' or equivalent incident index in srchIndexesAllowed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the SIEM RBAC configuration files to enumerate role-to-index permission mappings. For Splunk, review authorize.conf to identify which roles have access to incident-related indexes.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 10 'srchIndexesAllowed\|srchIndexesDefault' /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/authorize.conf | grep -B2 'notable\|siem\|incident'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only roles named with security-specific identifiers (soc_analyst, ir_team) have notable_events in their allowed index list.

option_description: An enumerated list of all organizational roles — beyond the dedicated security team — that hold read or write permissions to raw SIEM incident data, including full incident records, IOC feeds, and analyst investigation notes. This includes roles such as IT Operations, Helpdesk, NOC, Management, Compliance, and Audit.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'excessive_access_to_raw_incident_data' when this list is non-empty, access scope is 'full_raw', and need-to-know justification is not enforced. Each non-security role with raw access represents a potential insider threat vector or accidental disclosure path for active investigation details, attacker TTPs, and victim data. Directly maps to MITRE T1213 (Data from Information Repositories) where privileged insiders or compromised non-security accounts can enumerate full incident repositories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Microsoft Sentinel, enumerate all role assignments on the Log Analytics Workspace and filter out known security team groups to identify non-security roles with access.
how_to_obtain.command: az role assignment list --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/<workspace> --output json | jq -r '.[] | select(.principalName | test("SOC|SecurityTeam|IR_Team") | not) | [.principalName, .roleDefinitionName] | @csv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty list or list containing only explicitly approved exceptions with documented justification; any IT Operations, Helpdesk, or NOC entries require investigation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM platform's user and role management API to enumerate all principals with incident data permissions. For Splunk, query the roles endpoint and cross-reference with the incident index permissions.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS 'https://<splunk>:8089/services/authentication/users?count=-1&output_mode=json' | python3 -c "import sys,json; users=json.load(sys.stdin)['entry']; [print(u['name'], u['content'].get('roles','')) for u in users]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: User-to-role mapping showing only security-designated roles for users with access to incident data indexes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, navigate to Settings > Access Controls > Users and filter by index access to 'notable_events'. In Microsoft Sentinel, go to the Log Analytics Workspace > Access Control (IAM) > Role Assignments and sort by role to identify non-security groups with SecurityReader or Contributor access.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Access Controls > Users (filter by notable_events index) | Sentinel: Log Analytics Workspace > IAM > Role Assignments > Filter by non-security groups
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Complete list of role names with access; populate the attribute with any roles that are not part of the dedicated security function (SOC, CIRT, Threat Intel).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the formal access control list from the SIEM administrator. Cross-reference with HR group membership to identify which organizational departments have members in SIEM access groups. Ask for the last access review date and any documented exceptions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A complete access roster with role names, department classification, and date access was granted; any non-security roles identified should be added to this attribute list.

option_description: Indicates whether the organization enforces a formal, documented need-to-know justification process before any role is granted access to raw SIEM incident data. This includes a business justification requirement, an approval workflow, and an audit trail of access grants — going beyond simple RBAC configuration to require active human approval.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'excessive_access_to_raw_incident_data' when non-security roles have access AND access scope is 'full_raw' AND this control is absent. Without a justification gate, roles accumulate SIEM access through routine IT provisioning processes without security review, creating a sprawling access footprint over time. This facilitates MITRE T1213 (Data from Information Repositories) by ensuring that any compromised non-security account can access full incident intelligence, and T1212 (Exploitation for Credential Access) where credentials harvested from incident records can be used in further attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request documentation of the SIEM access provisioning procedure. Verify whether an access request form requires a business justification field, whether a security manager or CISO must approve requests for incident data access, and whether approved justifications are stored in a ticketing system with the access grant record.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented access request procedure requiring written business justification, evidence of approval chain (ticket IDs linked to access grants), and periodic access reviews validating ongoing justification.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the IAM or identity governance platform (e.g., SailPoint, Saviynt, Azure AD Entitlement Management), navigate to the access package or role assignment policies for SIEM incident data roles and verify that an approval workflow with justification is configured.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure AD: Identity Governance > Entitlement Management > Access Packages > SIEM Incident Access > Policy > Approval Settings | SailPoint: Role Management > SIEM_Analyst > Access Request Policy > Require Justification
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Approval workflow enabled with a mandatory justification field; approval requires security manager sign-off before access is provisioned.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the identity governance API to inspect access policy configuration for SIEM-related roles and confirm justification requirements are enforced programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: az ad group member list --group 'SIEM-Incident-Access' --output table && az rest --method GET --uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/identityGovernance/entitlementManagement/accessPackages' --query 'value[?displayName==`SIEM Incident Access`].accessPackageAssignmentPolicies'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Access package policy shows 'isApprovalRequired: true' and 'justificationRequired: true' in the approval stage configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the ITSM or IAM ticketing system for SIEM access grants over the past 12 months. For each access grant to a non-security role, verify that a corresponding approval ticket with justification text exists and was reviewed by an authorized approver before access was provisioned.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Every SIEM access grant for non-security roles has a linked approval ticket with documented business justification and named approver; access grants without linked tickets indicate the control is not enforced.

option_description: Defines what tier of incident data non-security roles can view when access is granted — whether they see full raw incident records (including IOCs, TTPs, victim details, analyst notes), summarized or redacted views with sensitive fields removed, or have no access to incident data at all.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'excessive_access_to_raw_incident_data' when non-security roles exist, this is 'full_raw', and need-to-know justification is absent. Granting full raw access to IT operations or helpdesk roles means those roles can read active attacker C2 infrastructure, affected system hostnames, exploited CVEs, and victim identities — intelligence that dramatically expands blast radius if any of those accounts are compromised. T1213 (Data from Information Repositories) is directly enabled when broad roles can query the full incident data store without field-level restrictions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk ES, navigate to Settings > Access Controls > Roles and inspect which fields and transforms are accessible to non-security roles assigned to the notable_events index. Check if field-level security or summary index views are configured to restrict sensitive fields for non-SOC roles. In Sentinel, navigate to Log Analytics Workspace > Tables > SecurityIncident and inspect column-level security policies.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Access Controls > Roles > [non-security role] > Field Filtering Settings | Sentinel: Log Analytics > Tables > SecurityIncident > Column-Level Security
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-security roles show a restricted field set excluding IOC details, raw log data, analyst notes, and victim PII; or no access at all to SecurityIncident table.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Microsoft Sentinel, use the Azure REST API to inspect table-level and column-level access restrictions on the SecurityIncident table for non-security role assignments.
how_to_obtain.command: az monitor log-analytics workspace table show --resource-group <rg> --workspace-name <workspace> --name SecurityIncident --output json | jq '.properties | {plan, retentionInDays, schema: .schema.columns | map(.name)}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Column restrictions or separate summary table configuration visible; absence of column-level security on SecurityIncident for broad roles indicates full_raw access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk, test the data visibility of a non-security role by impersonating it through the search API and running a query against the notable_events index to determine which fields are returned.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u it_operations_testuser:$TEST_PASS 'https://<splunk>:8089/services/search/jobs' -d 'search=search index=notable_events | head 1 | fields *&output_mode=json' | python3 -c "import sys,json; r=json.load(sys.stdin); print(list(r.get('results',[{}])[0].keys()) if 'results' in r else 'No results - check job')"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Fields returned should be limited to a pre-approved summary set; presence of 'src_ip', 'dest', 'analyst_notes', 'ioc_value', 'cve_id' fields indicates full_raw access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request a demonstration of what non-security roles see in the SIEM interface. Ask the SIEM administrator to log in as an IT Operations or Helpdesk role and show which incident fields, dashboards, and search indexes are accessible.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-security role shows only a summary dashboard with ticket status and priority; no raw log fields, IOCs, analyst notes, or victim-identifying information visible.

option_description: Controls whether the SIEM platform automatically masks, hashes, or pseudonymizes PII fields — including usernames, email addresses, IP addresses, and device identifiers — before writing incident records or associated logs to persistent storage. Determines if masking is platform-enforced at ingestion or left to analyst discretion.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'pii_not_masked_in_incident_records' when masking is disabled AND either plaintext PII fields are present OR role restriction is unrestricted. Without enforced masking, every incident record becomes a PII repository accessible to anyone with SIEM read access, creating GDPR, HIPAA, and CCPA exposure. MITRE T1589.003 (Employee Names) and T1589.002 (Email Addresses) are enabled when plaintext identities are stored in queryable incident logs, and T1654 (Log Enumeration) allows systematic PII harvesting from incident records at scale.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the SIEM ingestion pipeline configuration for masking or anonymization processors. For Splunk, review transforms.conf and props.conf for SEDCMD or lookup-based masking rules. For Elastic SIEM, inspect ingest pipeline configurations for redact or fingerprint processors.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'SEDCMD\|mask\|anon\|hash\|redact\|pseudonym' /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/transforms.conf /opt/splunk/etc/apps/*/local/transforms.conf
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SEDCMD rules matching email, username, IP, or device ID field patterns with replacement masks present; absence indicates no platform-level masking.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Elastic SIEM, query the Elasticsearch API to list ingest pipelines and check for redact or fingerprint processors applied to security incident indexes.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:$ES_PASS https://<elastic-host>:9200/_ingest/pipeline?pretty | python3 -c "import sys,json; pipes=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(k, [p.get('type') for p in v.get('processors',[])]) for k,v in pipes.items() if 'security' in k.lower() or 'incident' in k.lower()]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'redact', 'fingerprint', or 'script' processors present in the security incident ingest pipeline; absence confirms masking is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk, navigate to Settings > Fields > Field Transforms and search for masking transforms. In Microsoft Sentinel, navigate to Settings > Workspace Settings > Data Masking or Microsoft Purview compliance portal to check if dynamic data masking rules are applied to SecurityIncident or relevant custom tables.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Fields > Field Transforms (search 'mask' or 'anon') | Sentinel: Microsoft Purview > Data Map > SIEM Workspace > Dynamic Data Masking Rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active masking transforms configured for email_address, username, src_ip, dest_ip, and device_id fields in incident-related data models.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Sample 10-20 recent SIEM incident records from the storage layer (index or table) and inspect the raw field values for PII categories to determine whether masking is active.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS 'https://<splunk>:8089/services/search/jobs/export' -d 'search=search index=notable_events earliest=-7d | head 20 | table src_user, src_ip, dest, user, email&output_mode=csv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Fields show masked values (e.g., 'u***@domain.com', '10.x.x.x', 'ANON_USER_a3f2') rather than plaintext PII; unmasked readable values confirm pii_masking_enforced = false.

option_description: An enumerated list of PII field categories that have been confirmed — through direct inspection of stored incident records — to exist in plaintext without masking, hashing, or tokenization. Categories include user_identity (usernames, display names), ip_address (source/destination IPs), email_address, and device_identifier (hostnames, MAC addresses, asset IDs).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'pii_not_masked_in_incident_records' when masking is not enforced AND this list is non-empty. Each field category in this list represents a confirmed data protection gap — plaintext PII queryable by any role with SIEM read access. This creates direct regulatory violations under GDPR Article 25 (data protection by design) and enables MITRE T1654 (Log Enumeration) where adversaries systematically query incident logs to build identity profiles. Email addresses in plaintext enable T1589.002 targeted phishing against affected individuals identified in security incidents.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM incident index directly and inspect field values for each PII category to determine which are stored in plaintext. Run targeted searches for each category against a sample of recent incidents.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS 'https://<splunk>:8089/services/search/jobs/export' -d 'search=search index=notable_events earliest=-30d | head 50 | eval has_user=if(match(src_user,"[a-zA-Z0-9]+"),"PLAINTEXT","MASKED"), has_email=if(match(user,"@"),"PLAINTEXT","MASKED"), has_ip=if(match(src_ip,"^[0-9]{1,3}\\."),"PLAINTEXT","MASKED") | stats values(has_user) as user_status, values(has_email) as email_status, values(has_ip) as ip_status&output_mode=csv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each field category returns 'PLAINTEXT' if stored without masking or 'MASKED' if properly protected; all 'PLAINTEXT' results should be added to this attribute list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Export a representative sample (minimum 20 records) of raw SIEM incident tickets or log entries from the past 30 days and manually inspect each PII-relevant field. Check src_user, user, email, src_ip, dest_ip, src_mac, hostname, and device_id fields for readable plaintext values.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u admin:$SPLUNK_PASS 'https://<splunk>:8089/services/search/jobs/export' -d 'search=search index=notable_events earliest=-30d | head 20 | table _time, src_user, src_ip, dest_ip, user, email, src_mac, hostname, device_id&output_mode=csv' | head -25
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CSV output where each column is inspected: readable email addresses → add 'email_address'; readable usernames → add 'user_identity'; readable IPs → add 'ip_address'; readable hostnames/MACs → add 'device_identifier'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Elastic SIEM, query the security incident index using the Elasticsearch search API with field existence filters to identify which PII field types contain readable plaintext data in stored documents.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -u elastic:$ES_PASS 'https://<elastic>:9200/.siem-signals-*/_search?pretty' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size": 20, "_source": ["user.name","source.ip","destination.ip","user.email","host.name","host.mac"], "query": {"match_all": {}}}' | jq '.hits.hits[]._source'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON documents showing field values; presence of readable email strings, dotted-decimal IPs, or recognizable usernames in respective fields confirms those categories are stored in plaintext.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request a data mapping exercise from the SIEM administrator: for each field in the incident schema that could contain PII, document whether a masking transform is applied. Cross-reference the field list (src_user, user, email, src_ip, dest_ip, hostname, device_id, mac_address) with the active masking configuration to identify any unprotected categories.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A field-by-field audit matrix showing which PII categories have confirmed masking applied and which do not; unmasked categories should be recorded in this attribute.

option_description: Controls whether a formal, documented retention schedule exists specifically for SIEM-derived incident records, covering both minimum and maximum retention periods. This is a governance gate that determines whether downstream retention enforcement is even possible.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'undefined_retention_policy_for_incident_records' exposure immediately when retention_policy_defined is false. Without a documented policy, there is no basis for enforcing disposal schedules, creating indefinite accumulation of sensitive investigation records (IOCs, attacker TTPs, victim identities) and both over-retention and under-retention evidentiary risks. Verbal or informal practices explicitly do not satisfy this control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the organization's data governance or information security policy documentation set. Locate the section covering SIEM, SOC, or security incident data retention. Confirm the document explicitly names SIEM-derived incident records, specifies both minimum and maximum retention bounds, and has been formally approved (version-controlled, owner-signed, or committee-ratified).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A dated, approved policy document containing a named retention schedule for SIEM incident data with explicit day/month bounds and ownership attribution.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the organization's GRC or policy management platform (e.g., ServiceNow GRC, Archer, Confluence policy space). Search for 'SIEM retention', 'incident data retention', or 'security records schedule'. Verify the document status is 'Active' and not expired or in draft.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GRC Platform > Policy Library > Search: 'SIEM retention' OR 'incident data retention'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active, approved policy document with a status of 'Published' or equivalent, not 'Draft' or 'Under Review'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the SIEM or SOAR platform has a retention configuration file or embedded policy reference. For Splunk, inspect indexes.conf for retention directives and cross-reference against a written policy. For Elastic, review the ILM policy JSON. Confirm these settings are backed by a written governance document, not just platform defaults.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/indexes.conf | grep -E 'frozenTimePeriodInSecs|maxTotalDataSizeMB'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Retention directives present in platform config that match values stated in the written retention policy document.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Elastic ILM API to retrieve the current lifecycle policy applied to incident indices. Compare the returned policy phases and min_age values against the written retention schedule to confirm alignment.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'https://<elastic-host>:9200/_ilm/policy/siem-incident-policy' -H 'Authorization: ApiKey <key>' | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response showing policy phases (hot, warm, cold, delete) with min_age values that correspond to documented retention bounds.

option_description: Specifies the maximum number of days SIEM incident records are retained before scheduled disposal, as stated in policy. A value of 0 indicates no upper bound has been defined (indefinite retention), which is a configuration failure state.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'undefined_retention_policy_for_incident_records' exposure when retention_policy_defined is true but retention_period_days equals 0, treating indefinite retention as equivalent to having no policy. Indefinite retention maximizes the exposure window for sensitive investigation data. Common regulatory frameworks (GDPR Article 5(1)(e), NIST SP 800-61) require proportionate retention. A non-zero value paired with legal hold integration is required to clear the exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the formal retention policy document identified for retention_policy_defined. Locate the specific maximum retention duration for SIEM incident records expressed in days, months, or years. Convert to days for this attribute. If the policy states 'as needed' or 'indefinitely', record 0.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric value in days (e.g., 365, 730, 1825) explicitly stated in the approved retention policy document.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Splunk, navigate to Settings > Indexes > Select the incident index > Review 'Frozen data retention period'. In Microsoft Sentinel, go to Settings > Workspace Settings > Data Retention. In IBM QRadar, navigate to Admin > System Settings > Data Retention. Record the configured maximum in days.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Indexes > [incident_index] > Archiving | Sentinel: Settings > Workspace Settings > Data Retention | QRadar: Admin > System Settings > Data Retention
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric retention value in days visible in the platform UI that matches the written policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Splunk deployments, query the index metadata to retrieve the configured frozenTimePeriodInSecs value and convert to days. For Elastic, retrieve ILM policy delete phase min_age.
how_to_obtain.command: splunk search 'index=_internal | rest /services/data/indexes | table title frozenTimePeriodInSecs | eval retention_days=frozenTimePeriodInSecs/86400' -auth admin:password 2>/dev/null || curl -s 'https://<elastic>:9200/_ilm/policy/siem-incidents' | python3 -c "import sys,json; p=json.load(sys.stdin); print(p.get('siem-incidents',{}).get('policy',{}).get('phases',{}).get('delete',{}).get('min_age','not set'))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric value in seconds (Splunk) or age string (Elastic) that converts to the policy-stated retention period in days.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For QRadar or on-premises SIEM, inspect the retention configuration file or database settings. For Splunk, read frozenTimePeriodInSecs from indexes.conf and divide by 86400 to obtain days.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'frozenTimePeriodInSecs|maxDataRetentionDays|retentionDays' /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/indexes.conf /etc/qradar/retention.conf 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A configuration directive with a numeric value that, when converted to days, matches the documented policy maximum.

option_description: Indicates whether the SIEM or associated data store has a mechanism to apply legal holds that pause automated deletion of incident records when litigation, regulatory investigation, or eDiscovery requires preservation beyond the standard retention period.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'undefined_retention_policy_for_incident_records' even when retention_policy_defined is true and retention_period_days is non-zero if legal_hold_integration_configured is false. This is because automated deletion schedules operating without a hold override mechanism can destroy evidentiary data subject to litigation holds, creating spoliation risk. Legal hold integration is the third required element alongside a defined policy and a bounded retention period.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Sentinel or Microsoft Purview, navigate to Compliance Portal > eDiscovery > Core or Purview > Data Lifecycle Management > Holds. Verify that holds can be applied to Log Analytics workspaces or Sentinel incident records. In Splunk, check whether Splunk Legal Hold or a third-party eDiscovery connector is configured under Apps.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Purview Compliance Portal > eDiscovery > Core > Holds | Splunk: Apps > Manage Apps > Search 'Legal Hold' | ServiceNow: Legal Hold > Active Holds
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A configured hold policy or connector that covers the SIEM data source, with at least one active or available hold template.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Microsoft Purview Compliance API to list active retention holds covering the Log Analytics workspace used by Sentinel, confirming programmatic hold capability exists.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -X GET 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/compliance/ediscovery/cases' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response listing eDiscovery cases or holds; check that at least one targets the SIEM workspace. An empty list or 403 indicates no hold integration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the legal, compliance, or SOC manager to determine whether a documented legal hold procedure exists that names the SIEM platform and specifies how holds are triggered (workflow ticket, email trigger, API call). Request evidence of at least one past hold event on SIEM data. Undocumented or untested procedures do not qualify.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A written legal hold procedure referencing the SIEM, and evidence of at least one successfully applied hold (e.g., hold ticket, audit log entry).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Elastic deployments, verify that an ILM policy with a freeze or hold action exists, or that Elastic's snapshot lifecycle management is configured to preserve indices upon hold trigger. Review the policy JSON for a 'frozen' phase or custom action preventing deletion.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s 'https://<elastic-host>:9200/_ilm/policy' -H 'Authorization: ApiKey <key>' | python3 -c "import sys,json; policies=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(k) for k,v in policies.items() if 'frozen' in str(v) or 'searchable_snapshot' in str(v)]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one ILM policy name printed, indicating a freeze or hold-compatible phase is defined for SIEM data indices.

option_description: Controls whether encryption at rest is actively enforced on the storage system hosting SIEM incident data, including shared drives, ticketing systems, and SIEM export repositories. This attribute distinguishes between encryption being available versus actively enforced for the relevant storage locations.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'unencrypted_incident_data_at_rest_in_shared_repositories' when encryption_at_rest_enabled is false and the storage type is not a dedicated_secure_repository, or when encryption is absent regardless of access controls. Unencrypted incident data in shared repositories means that if storage access controls fail or the repository is compromised, full incident contents including attacker methodologies, IOCs, and affected asset details are exposed in plaintext. This maps to MITRE T1213 and T1530.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob, GCP GCS): verify server-side encryption is enforced via bucket/container policy, not just enabled as default. AWS: S3 > Bucket > Properties > Default Encryption. Azure: Storage Account > Encryption. GCP: Cloud Storage > Bucket > Configuration > Encryption. For shared drives (Windows file server), check BitLocker status via Server Manager.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS: S3 > [bucket] > Properties > Server-side encryption | Azure: Storage Account > Encryption > Enabled | GCP: Cloud Storage > [bucket] > Configuration > Encryption type
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Encryption status showing 'Enabled' with a key management option (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, AES-256, CMEK) for the specific buckets or containers holding incident data.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check AWS S3 bucket encryption enforcement for the incident data bucket, and verify a bucket policy exists that denies unencrypted PutObject requests.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-bucket-encryption --bucket <incident-data-bucket> 2>&1 && aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <incident-data-bucket> | python3 -c "import sys,json; p=json.load(sys.stdin); print(p.get('Policy','No policy'))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration showing AES256 or aws:kms, and a bucket policy with a Deny condition on s3:PutObject without encryption headers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows-based shared drives hosting incident exports, check BitLocker encryption status on the volume. For Linux-based storage, check LUKS encryption status.
how_to_obtain.command: manage-bde -status <DriveLetter>: 2>/dev/null || cryptsetup status /dev/mapper/<volume_name> 2>/dev/null || lsblk -f | grep -E 'crypt|LUKS'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: BitLocker output showing 'Protection Status: Protection On' or cryptsetup output showing 'type: LUKS' with active status.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Azure REST API to confirm encryption is enabled and enforced on the Storage Account used for incident data, including the key source (Microsoft-managed or customer-managed).
how_to_obtain.command: az storage account show --name <storage-account> --resource-group <rg> --query 'encryption' -o json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON showing 'services.blob.enabled: true', 'services.file.enabled: true', and 'keySource: Microsoft.Storage' or 'Microsoft.Keyvault' for customer-managed keys.

option_description: Identifies the type of repository where incident summaries, analyst notes, and SIEM exports are stored. This classification drives risk evaluation because different storage types carry different inherent security properties and exposure surfaces.
security_impact: The Rego policy evaluates this attribute within the 'unencrypted_incident_data_at_rest_in_shared_repositories' rule — specifically, 'dedicated_secure_repository' is the only storage type excluded from the exposure trigger when encryption is absent. All other types (shared_network_drive, ticketing_system, cloud_storage_bucket, email_or_collaboration_tool) remain exposed to the full rule logic. Storage in email_or_collaboration_tool is particularly dangerous as it typically lacks both encryption enforcement and granular ACLs for sensitive security intelligence.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview SOC analysts and the security operations manager to enumerate all locations where incident reports, analyst notes, SIEM exports, and forensic findings are stored. Ask specifically about ad-hoc storage (email attachments, Teams channels, personal OneDrive) in addition to official systems. Document each location type found.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A complete inventory of storage locations with their types (network drive path, ticketing system name, S3 bucket name, etc.) that can be mapped to the enum values.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM platform (Splunk, Sentinel, QRadar), navigate to reporting or export settings and identify configured export destinations. In the SOAR platform or ticketing system (Jira, ServiceNow), check the attachment or file storage configuration to identify the backend repository type.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Forwarding and Receiving > Forward Data | ServiceNow: System Definition > Attachment Configuration | Jira: Settings > System > Attachments
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Identification of the storage backend type (e.g., NFS share path, S3 bucket ARN, database-native storage, or email relay) used by the incident management toolchain.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify mounted network shares on SOC workstations or SIEM servers that may be used for incident data storage. Check for SIEM export directories and their underlying storage type.
how_to_obtain.command: mount | grep -E 'cifs|nfs|smb' 2>/dev/null; df -hT | grep -E 'nfs|cifs|fuse'; ls -la /opt/splunk/var/lib/splunk/export_jobs/ 2>/dev/null; find /mnt /share /data -name '*.csv' -o -name '*.json' -o -name '*incident*' 2>/dev/null | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Mount points showing cifs/nfs (shared_network_drive), no mounts with data in local application dirs (dedicated_secure_repository), or S3 FUSE mounts (cloud_storage_bucket).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM audit logs or DLP logs for file transfer or export events that reveal where incident data is being sent or saved. In Splunk, search the _audit index for export activity. In Sentinel, query the AzureActivity or OfficeActivity tables for data exports.
how_to_obtain.command: splunk search 'index=_audit action=search export earliest=-30d | stats count by user search_id savedsearch_name | head 20' -auth admin:password 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Audit log entries showing export destinations or file write paths that identify the storage location type in use.

option_description: Indicates whether role-based or need-to-know access controls are actively enforced on the repository storing SIEM incident data, restricting access to named individuals or security roles rather than broad groups such as 'Everyone', 'Domain Users', or 'Authenticated Users'.
security_impact: The Rego policy incorporates access_control_enforced in the 'unencrypted_incident_data_at_rest_in_shared_repositories' rule — when encryption is absent AND access controls are not enforced, the exposure fires regardless of storage type. Without enforced ACLs, any authenticated user who can reach the file share, ticketing system, or storage bucket can read sensitive investigation data including IOCs, attacker TTPs, and victim identities. This maps to MITRE T1213 (Data from Information Repositories).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Windows shared drives, enumerate the NTFS ACLs and share-level permissions on the incident data directory. Identify any broad groups (Everyone, Domain Users, Authenticated Users, BUILTIN\Users) that grant read or write access.
how_to_obtain.command: icacls '\\<server>\<incident_share>' 2>/dev/null; net share <share_name> 2>/dev/null; Get-Acl '\\<server>\<incident_share>' | Format-List | Out-String
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL output showing only named security roles (SOC_Analysts, Incident_Responders, Security_Managers) with no broad group grants. Broad group presence indicates access_control_enforced = false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS S3 buckets storing incident exports, verify the bucket ACL and policy deny public access and restrict GetObject to specific IAM roles or principals only.
how_to_obtain.command: aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket <incident-bucket> && aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <incident-bucket> | python3 -c "import sys,json; p=json.loads(json.load(sys.stdin)['Policy']); [print(s) for s in p['Statement']]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL showing no public grants (no AllUsers or AuthenticatedUsers grantees), and bucket policy restricting s3:GetObject to specific IAM role ARNs representing the security team.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the ticketing system (Jira, ServiceNow): navigate to Project Settings > Permissions (Jira) or Application Access > Roles (ServiceNow) and verify that the security incident project or table is restricted to the security team group, not all authenticated users. Check that no 'Any logged in user' or 'Any' permission entries exist for Browse or Read.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Jira: Project Settings > Permissions > Browse Projects permission | ServiceNow: Security Incident > Application Access > roles with read access | SharePoint: Site Settings > Site Permissions
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Permission entries listing only named security groups (SOC, CSIRT, Security Managers) for read/browse access, with no global authenticated user groups present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Azure RBAC assignments on the Storage Account or Container used for incident data to verify only security-scoped roles (not Contributor or broad Reader) have data plane access.
how_to_obtain.command: az role assignment list --scope /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/<account>/blobServices/default/containers/<container> -o table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Role assignment table listing only specific principal names or security group IDs with 'Storage Blob Data Reader' or custom roles, no broad assignments to 'All Users' or subscription-level Reader roles.

option_description: Indicates whether SIEM incident records include personally identifiable information belonging to data subjects from regulated jurisdictions such as EU residents under GDPR or UK residents under UK GDPR. PII in this context includes user email addresses, IP addresses tied to regulated-jurisdiction residents, names, and device identifiers linked to identifiable individuals.
security_impact: This is the primary gating attribute for the 'cross_border_transfer_of_incident_data_without_compliance_review' Rego rule. When true and cross-border transfers exist without documented legal basis, the exposure fires. SIEM incident data routinely captures user identities (email addresses in authentication events, IP-to-user mappings in EDR telemetry) that constitute PII under GDPR Article 4(1). Misclassifying this as non-PII eliminates all downstream regulatory transfer controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the SIEM data schema and enrichment pipeline documentation. Identify fields present in incident records: user.email, source.ip, destination.ip, user.name, host.name, process.user, and any custom enrichment fields. Determine whether the organization has EU/UK employees or systems from which events originate. If yes, PII from regulated jurisdictions is almost certainly present.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A field inventory confirming presence or absence of user-identifiable fields (email, username, IP-to-user mapping) in incident records, with geographic scope of the user population documented.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Sample recent SIEM incident records to inspect for PII field presence. In Splunk, query the incident index for events containing email addresses or usernames. In Elastic, use a field caps query to enumerate mappable PII fields in the incident index.
how_to_obtain.command: splunk search 'index=notable OR index=incident earliest=-7d | fields user, src_user, user_email, src_ip, dest_ip, email | head 20' -auth admin:password 2>/dev/null || curl -s 'https://<elastic>:9200/siem-incident-*/_field_caps?fields=user*,email*,source.ip,destination.ip' -H 'Authorization: ApiKey <key>' | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E '"name"|"type"'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Sample records showing populated user, email, or IP fields, or field_caps response listing user.name, user.email, source.ip as indexed fields in incident indices.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM platform's incident or notable event view, open several representative incident records and inspect the visible fields. Check for user identity fields (username, email, employee ID), IP addresses that can be correlated to individuals, and device identifiers. Also check the enrichment or lookup configurations to see if IP-to-user or IP-to-country mappings are applied.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk ES: Incident Review > Notable Events > Select event > All Fields | Sentinel: Incidents > Select incident > Entities tab | QRadar: Offenses > Select offense > Contributing Events
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Incident detail view showing populated user identity or network address fields attributable to specific individuals. Presence of these fields for any EU/UK user population confirms true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM enrichment pipeline configurations (Logstash filters, Splunk transforms.conf, Elastic ingest pipelines) for lookups or grok patterns that add user identity context to events. Check whether GeoIP enrichment is applied and whether EU/UK IP ranges are represented in the incident data.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'user|email|geoip|country' /etc/logstash/conf.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null; cat /opt/splunk/etc/apps/*/lookups/identity*.csv 2>/dev/null | head -5; curl -s 'https://<elastic>:9200/_ingest/pipeline/siem-enrich' -H 'Authorization: ApiKey <key>' | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E 'geoip|user|email'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipeline configurations showing geoip processors with target_field containing country data, or identity lookup tables containing email/username fields, confirming PII enrichment is applied to incident records.

option_description: Enumerates the list of countries or regions to which SIEM incident data (including raw logs, IOC context, and analyst notes) is transferred. Common transfer vectors include MSSP SOC locations in other countries, cloud storage regions, SOAR webhook integrations with foreign endpoints, and threat intelligence sharing platforms.
security_impact: This array attribute is directly evaluated in the 'cross_border_transfer_of_incident_data_without_compliance_review' Rego rule. When count(cross_border_transfer_destinations) > 0 and incident_data_contains_pii_from_regulated_jurisdiction is true, the exposure fires unless legal basis is documented. Even with anonymization applied, the second Rego condition still triggers the exposure, meaning any non-empty transfer destination list combined with regulated PII creates a compliance finding under GDPR Chapter V transfer restrictions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review MSSP contracts and service delivery schedules to identify all SOC analyst locations. Review cloud service agreements and region configurations for storage services. Interview the SOC manager and procurement team to identify all third-party security service providers and their geographic delivery locations. Ask specifically about sub-processors and geographic redundancy configurations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of countries where MSSP analysts are located, cloud storage regions where incident data is replicated, and any threat intel sharing platforms with non-domestic endpoints.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM or SOAR platform, review all configured forwarding destinations, webhook endpoints, API integrations, and export targets. For each, identify the geographic location of the receiving endpoint. In AWS, check S3 bucket replication rules for cross-region or cross-account destinations. In Azure Sentinel, check Data Connectors and playbook Logic App connectors for external endpoints.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk: Settings > Forwarding and Receiving > Forward Data > Forwarding | Sentinel: Settings > Workspace Settings > Linked services + Logic Apps > HTTP connectors | AWS Console: S3 > [bucket] > Management > Replication rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of IP addresses, hostnames, or region identifiers for all forwarding destinations. Resolve hostnames to geolocate receiving countries using whois or ip-api.com.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect SIEM forwarder configuration files to enumerate all receiving endpoints. For Splunk Universal Forwarder or heavy forwarder, check outputs.conf. For Logstash, check output sections in pipeline configs. Resolve destination IPs to countries.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'server|host|endpoint|url' /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/outputs.conf 2>/dev/null; grep -A5 'output {' /etc/logstash/conf.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'hosts|url|endpoint'; curl -s 'https://ip-api.com/batch' -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '[{"query":"<resolved-destination-ip>"}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of destination hostnames or IPs from config files, with country attribution from geo-IP lookup (e.g., US, IN, PH, GB, DE). Any non-domestic country should be added to the array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS CloudTrail or Azure Monitor for recent data transfer or replication events that reveal where incident data has been sent, including cross-region S3 replication, Log Analytics workspace data export, and API calls to external security platforms.
how_to_obtain.command: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=ReplicateObject --start-time 2024-01-01 --query 'Events[*].{Time:EventTime,User:Username,Source:CloudTrailEvent}' --output table 2>/dev/null || az monitor log-analytics workspace data-export list --resource-group <rg> --workspace-name <ws> -o table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CloudTrail or Azure Monitor events showing replication or export destinations as S3 bucket ARNs in foreign regions or external URIs, which can be mapped to destination countries.

option_description: Controls whether a documented legal mechanism (SCCs, adequacy decision, Binding Corporate Rules, or equivalent) exists to authorize cross-border transfer of SIEM incident data containing PII from regulated jurisdictions. This is a compliance gate that must be established before any incident data leaves its jurisdiction of origin.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Cross Border Transfer Of Incident Data Without Compliance Review' exposure whenever incident data contains PII from a regulated jurisdiction and cross-border transfer destinations exist but data_transfer_legal_basis_documented is false — regardless of whether anonymization is applied. This means even pseudonymized transfers require documented legal basis. Without this attribute set to true, the organization faces regulatory violation risk under GDPR or equivalent frameworks independent of the security investigation's legitimacy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the organization's data protection register or Records of Processing Activities (RoPA) and locate entries referencing SIEM, incident management, or security telemetry. Confirm whether each cross-border transfer destination (e.g., MSSP headquarters, cloud SIEM region) has an associated SCC, adequacy reliance note, or BCR reference attached to the record.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each cross-border transfer destination is listed with a specific legal mechanism identifier (e.g., 'EU SCCs 2021 — Module 1 signed 2023-04-12') and the data categories covered include security incident telemetry and PII.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Locate and review executed DPA or MSSP contracts stored in the legal document repository. Search for SCC annexes, data transfer impact assessments (DTIAs), or adequacy reliance clauses that explicitly name incident data or security telemetry as a covered data category.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -ri 'standard contractual\|adequacy\|binding corporate\|data transfer agreement\|incident data' /path/to/contracts/ --include='*.pdf' --include='*.docx' -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one contract file returned per active cross-border transfer destination, each containing SCC annexes or adequacy clauses with incident/security data categories explicitly scoped.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If the organization uses a GRC or privacy management platform (e.g., OneTrust, TrustArc, ServiceNow GRC), query the transfer records API to retrieve documented transfer mechanisms for the SIEM or incident management data processing activity.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GRC_TOKEN' 'https://<grc-platform>/api/v1/processing-activities?category=security-incident&transfers=true' | jq '.[] | {destination, legal_mechanism, signed_date, data_categories}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response listing each transfer destination with fields: legal_mechanism (e.g., 'SCCs_2021'), signed_date populated, and data_categories including 'security_incident' or 'PII'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the privacy management platform or legal contract repository portal (e.g., OneTrust > Data Inventory > Data Flows, or SharePoint legal folder). Filter for the SIEM or security operations processing activity and inspect each international data flow for attached transfer mechanism documentation.
how_to_obtain.navigation: OneTrust > Data Inventory > Processing Activities > [SIEM/Incident Management] > Data Flows > International Transfers > Legal Basis column
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each cross-border flow entry shows a non-empty legal basis field with a document attachment (SCC, BCR, or adequacy note) rather than 'None' or 'Pending'.

typical_values: null (undetermined — common in organizations that haven't explicitly scoped MSSP transfers in their DPA)

option_description: Controls whether PII fields embedded in SIEM incident records (user identities, IP addresses, email addresses, device identifiers) are anonymized or pseudonymized to prevent re-identification before any cross-border transmission occurs. This applies to SIEM export pipelines, SOAR playbook outputs, and MSSP data sharing integrations.
security_impact: The Rego policy evaluates pii_anonymization_applied_before_transfer as a secondary safeguard in the 'Cross Border Transfer Of Incident Data Without Compliance Review' rule. Critically, the policy fires even when anonymization IS applied if legal basis documentation is absent — confirming anonymization alone does not substitute for legal compliance. However, when both legal basis is absent AND anonymization is false, the exposure is triggered unconditionally. This attribute must be true to reduce regulatory risk surface and protect victim identity during international incident investigations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SIEM export pipeline configuration files and SOAR playbook definitions to identify whether PII field transformation steps (masking, hashing, redaction) are applied before data is forwarded to cross-border destinations. Check pipeline-level transform rules in tools such as Logstash, Cribl, or Splunk Heavy Forwarder.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'mask|hash|redact|anonymi[sz]|pseudonym|sha256|md5' /etc/logstash/conf.d/ /opt/cribl/config/ --include='*.conf' --include='*.yml' -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration files returned that contain masking or hashing filters applied to fields such as src_user, dest_ip, email, or username prior to output stages targeting cross-border destinations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SOAR platform (e.g., Splunk SOAR, Palo Alto XSOAR, Tines), open playbooks that handle incident data sharing with MSSPs or external analysts. Inspect each action block for data transformation steps that sanitize or pseudonymize PII fields before the data is sent via API or file transfer.
how_to_obtain.navigation: XSOAR > Playbooks > [MSSP Data Share / Incident Export Playbook] > Action blocks > inspect 'Set Field' or 'Transform' steps before 'HTTP Request' or 'Email' output actions
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Playbook actions show explicit field-level masking (e.g., replace email with SHA-256 hash, redact username to 'REDACTED') applied in steps immediately preceding any cross-border data transmission action.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SOC team lead or SIEM architect to confirm whether documented anonymization procedures exist and are enforced. Request the data handling runbook for MSSP escalations and verify it explicitly lists which PII fields are transformed and by what method (hashing algorithm, redaction pattern, tokenization) before transfer.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Runbook document exists with a dedicated 'PII Sanitization Before Transfer' section listing specific fields (e.g., src_user, email, hostname) and the transformation method applied, with evidence of enforcement (e.g., automated pipeline step or pre-send checklist sign-off).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Pull a sample of incident records from the SIEM export or MSSP sharing log and inspect the actual data transmitted. Verify that PII fields appear as hashes, tokens, or redacted placeholders rather than plaintext values in the exported payload.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /var/log/siem/exports/mssp_transfer_$(date +%Y%m%d).json | jq '.[0:5] | .[] | {src_user, email, src_ip, hostname}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows PII fields as hashed values (e.g., 'src_user': 'a3f2c1...') or '[REDACTED]' strings, with no plaintext usernames, email addresses, or personally identifiable hostnames present.

typical_values: false (most common — MSSP integrations often transfer raw incident JSON without dedicated PII transformation stages)
true (mature organizations with dedicated DLP pipeline stages or SOAR-enforced sanitization playbooks)

option_description: Controls whether a formal, certified destruction or secure deletion procedure is mandated and enforced when closed SIEM incident records are disposed of. This procedure must cover all storage locations — primary SIEM/ticketing systems, backup systems, and any exported copies — and require a certificate of destruction or equivalent audit record as evidence of completion.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the 'Insecure Disposal Of Closed Incident Records' exposure when certified_destruction_procedure_enforced is false, treating absence of this control as an unconditional misconfiguration. Even if residual_data_locations_addressed is true, a false value for this attribute still triggers the exposure independently. Without certified destruction, historical incident records containing previously exploited vulnerabilities, compromised credential references, and attacker TTPs remain recoverable from backup snapshots or soft-deleted storage, enabling adversary reconnaissance of the organization's security history.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the data retention and disposal policy document and incident record closure runbook. Verify whether the policy explicitly mandates a certified destruction step (with sign-off or certificate of destruction) as a required gate before an incident record is considered fully disposed of, and confirm the policy names the responsible role.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy document contains a section titled 'Certified Destruction' or 'Secure Deletion' with: mandatory sign-off requirement, named responsible role (e.g., SOC Manager), certificate of destruction template reference, and coverage of primary system, backups, and exports.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the ITSM or incident ticketing system (e.g., ServiceNow, Jira Service Management), navigate to the incident closure workflow configuration. Inspect whether a 'Data Destruction Certification' approval step or mandatory field capturing destruction sign-off exists as a required gate in the closure state transition.
how_to_obtain.navigation: ServiceNow > Process Flow Editor > Incident > Closure Transition > Required Fields / Approval Steps > check for 'Data Destruction Certified' mandatory field or approver block
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Workflow shows a mandatory approval or attestation step (not optional) requiring destruction certification before the incident record transitions to 'Closed/Purged' status.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the ITSM API to retrieve a sample of recently closed incident records and check whether a destruction certification timestamp or certificate reference field is populated, indicating the procedure was executed.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u '$SNOW_USER:$SNOW_PASS' 'https://<instance>.service-now.com/api/now/table/incident?sysparm_query=state=7&sysparm_fields=number,closed_at,u_destruction_cert_date,u_destruction_cert_ref&sysparm_limit=10' | jq '.result[] | {number, closed_at, destruction_cert_date: .u_destruction_cert_date, cert_ref: .u_destruction_cert_ref}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each closed incident record returns non-null values for destruction_cert_date and cert_ref fields, confirming the certified destruction step was completed and recorded.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review any automated disposal scripts or cron jobs configured to purge closed incident records. Confirm the script generates a destruction log entry or certificate artifact upon completion, and that the script is active and scheduled.
how_to_obtain.command: crontab -l | grep -i 'purge\|destroy\|dispose\|incident' && cat /opt/siem/scripts/incident_purge.sh | grep -E 'cert|log|audit|destroy'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cron entry exists for the purge script with a scheduled interval; script body contains logging or certificate generation code (e.g., writes to /var/log/incident_destruction.log with timestamp and record ID).

typical_values: false (predominant in organizations where incident records are soft-deleted without formal destruction workflows)
true (observed in organizations with ISO 27001 certification or regulatory mandates requiring documented destruction evidence)

option_description: Controls whether the organization's disposal procedures explicitly enumerate and address all residual data locations where closed incident records may persist beyond the primary deletion action. This includes recycle bins, backup snapshots, point-in-time recovery volumes, unmanaged exports, shared drive copies, and email attachments containing incident data.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Insecure Disposal Of Closed Incident Records' exposure specifically when certified_destruction_procedure_enforced is true but residual_data_locations_addressed is false — recognizing that a destruction procedure covering only primary systems is insufficient. Residual copies in backup snapshots or exported files containing historical vulnerability details, compromised credentials, and attacker methodologies represent recoverable intelligence for adversaries who gain access to backup storage or unmanaged file shares, directly enabling T1485 (Data Destruction evasion) and T1070.004 (File Deletion) recovery scenarios.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Obtain the incident record disposal runbook and data destruction policy. Review whether the document explicitly lists each residual data location category: backup snapshot schedules and purge timelines, recycle bin emptying procedures, export/download registries and their deletion steps, and shared drive or collaboration tool copies. Confirm each category has a defined remediation action, not just a general 'delete all copies' statement.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Runbook contains a checklist or table enumerating at minimum: (1) SIEM primary store, (2) backup snapshots with purge timeline, (3) recycle bin/soft-delete clearing, (4) export registry review and file deletion, (5) shared drive / collaboration platform copies — each with a specific action and responsible owner.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect backup retention configuration for the SIEM platform and ticketing system to determine snapshot retention periods and whether purge automation aligns with incident data disposal timelines. Confirm that backup schedules do not indefinitely retain incident data past its authorized retention period.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/backup/siem_backup.conf | grep -E 'retain|expire|purge|snapshot|ttl' && aws backup list-backup-plans --query 'BackupPlansList[?contains(BackupPlanName, `siem`) || contains(BackupPlanName, `incident`)].{Name:BackupPlanName,Id:BackupPlanId}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Backup configuration shows a defined expiration period for SIEM/incident data backups that matches or is shorter than the authorized retention period, and AWS Backup returns a plan with SIEM or incident data in scope with a deletion lifecycle rule.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SIEM platform (e.g., Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic SIEM) and ticketing system, navigate to the data management or storage settings. Verify whether recycle bin or soft-delete features are configured with an automatic purge interval, and that the interval is consistent with the disposal policy.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk > Settings > Indexes > [incident index] > Frozen Path and Max Time settings | ServiceNow > System Properties > Cleanup Schedules > Incident records recycle bin TTL
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Splunk index shows a maxTotalDataSizeMB and frozenTimePeriodInSecs consistent with retention policy; ServiceNow shows a recycle bin auto-purge schedule configured to run within the policy-defined disposal window.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review disposal execution logs or destruction certificates from previous incident record closures to verify that residual location checks were actually performed. Look for log entries referencing backup purge confirmations, export file deletions, and recycle bin clearance as part of completed disposal workflows.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'backup_purged|export_deleted|recycle_cleared|snapshot_removed|residual' /var/log/incident_destruction.log | tail -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries for recent closure events contain lines confirming each residual location was addressed (e.g., 'backup_purged: true', 'export_deleted: 3 files', 'recycle_cleared: confirmed') rather than only a primary deletion entry.

typical_values: false (very common — most disposal procedures address primary system deletion only, with backup and export residuals overlooked)
true (found in organizations with explicit data destruction checklists enforced through ITSM workflow mandatory fields)

option_description: Captures the current operational status of the organization's documented retention and disposal policy specifically governing closed SIEM incident records. The three states reflect whether the policy is absent entirely, documented but not operationally enforced, or actively enforced through technical controls and procedural compliance.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'Insecure Disposal Of Closed Incident Records' exposure for both 'absent' and 'documented_not_enforced' status values — treating a paper policy without enforcement as equivalent to having no policy. Only 'enforced' status satisfies this control. This directly addresses both over-retention risk (indefinite storage of sensitive investigation records expanding the exposure window for T1565.001 Stored Data Manipulation) and under-retention risk (premature deletion before legal hold satisfaction, impairing forensic investigations per T1070.004). The policy status gates the entire lifecycle governance of incident records.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the information security policy library and data governance register. Locate the policy document specifically governing SIEM or incident ticketing data retention. Assess its status: confirm it has been formally approved (dated signature from appropriate authority), determine whether it specifies concrete retention periods and disposal methods for incident records, and verify it is within its review cycle (not expired).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy document found with: approval signature and date within review cycle, explicit retention period stated in days/years for closed incident records, named disposal method (secure deletion, certified destruction), and scope statement covering SIEM and ticketing platforms. If document exists but lacks these elements or has no evidence of enforcement, classify as 'documented_not_enforced'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the ITSM or SIEM platform, check whether automated retention enforcement controls exist that correspond to the documented policy. For example, in Splunk verify index data age limits; in ServiceNow confirm scheduled purge jobs for closed incidents are active and aligned to the policy period.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Splunk > Settings > Indexes > [incident index] > Review 'Max time' (frozenTimePeriodInSecs) value | ServiceNow > System Scheduler > Active Jobs > search for 'incident' purge or cleanup jobs > verify Last Run and Next Run timestamps
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Splunk index frozenTimePeriodInSecs value matches the policy-specified retention period converted to seconds; ServiceNow shows an active scheduled job for incident record cleanup with a recent 'Last Run' timestamp — confirming enforcement. Absence of these controls or mismatch with policy indicates 'documented_not_enforced'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM index or ticketing system database to check the age distribution of closed incident records. If records exist significantly beyond the documented retention period, the policy is documented but not enforced. If no records exceed the retention period, enforcement may be active.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Splunk: Check for closed incidents older than retention period (e.g., 730 days)
splunk search 'index=incident_records status=closed earliest=-5y latest=-730d | stats count by _time' -auth admin:$PASS -uri https://localhost:8089

# ServiceNow API: find closed incidents older than 2 years
curl -s -u '$SNOW_USER:$SNOW_PASS' 'https://<instance>.service-now.com/api/now/table/incident?sysparm_query=state=7^closed_atRELATIVELT@year@ago@2&sysparm_fields=number,closed_at&sysparm_limit=5' | jq '.result | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Splunk returns zero results for incidents closed beyond the retention period, or ServiceNow API returns 0 records older than the policy window — indicating active enforcement. Non-zero counts indicate 'documented_not_enforced'. No policy document found at all indicates 'absent'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect SIEM platform index configuration files and any automated lifecycle management scripts to determine whether retention limits are technically configured and match the documented policy period.
how_to_obtain.command:
cat /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/indexes.conf | grep -A 20 '\[incident\|\[siem\|\[security_incidents' | grep -E 'maxTotalDataSizeMB|frozenTimePeriodInSecs|coldToFrozenDir|homePath'

# Convert frozenTimePeriodInSecs to days for comparison with policy
python3 -c "print($(grep frozenTimePeriodInSecs /opt/splunk/etc/system/local/indexes.conf | awk -F= '{print $2}' | tr -d ' ') / 86400, 'days')"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Index configuration shows frozenTimePeriodInSecs value that, when converted to days, matches the retention period specified in the policy document (e.g., 63072000 seconds = 730 days = 2 years). Mismatch or missing configuration indicates 'documented_not_enforced'. File not found or no incident index configured indicates 'absent'.

typical_values: absent (common in small to mid-size organizations without dedicated data governance programs)
documented_not_enforced (frequent in organizations that have written policies as part of certification efforts but lack technical enforcement controls)
enforced (observed in regulated industries — financial services, healthcare — with active DLP, ITSM automation, and periodic compliance audits)
